extracted.intended_audience: communication scholars, journalism researchers, political scientists, and professional journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and empirical analysis of how mass media allocate voice to government and non-government actors (the 'indexing' hypothesis), with a content-analysis measurement approach applied to New York Times coverage of U.S. policy on Nicaragua. Useful for evaluating news balance and studying press–state dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural guideline for press-government relations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Culturally speaking, it is generally reasonable for journalists to grant government officials a privileged voice in the news, unless the range of official debate on a given topic excludes or ‘marginalizes’ stable majority opinion in society, and unless official actions raise doubts about political propriety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the official range of debate excludes stable majority opinion or when official actions raise doubts about propriety, the press should foreground other social voices (polls, opposition groups, academics, analysts) in news stories and editorials as checks against unrepresentative or irresponsible governments. This norm is proposed as a middle-ground standard drawn from competing U.S. political traditions and is intended as a basis for normative evaluation of journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing hypothesis (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mass media news professionals... tend to ‘index’ the range of voices and viewpoints in both news and editorials according to the range of views expressed in mainstream government debate about a given topic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing means journalists allow official debate to set the boundaries of legitimate news voices; non-official voices are included when similar opinions are present in official circles. The hypothesis explains why media often privilege official sources and provides a testable behavioral, structural, and attitudinal account of press-government relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: applies primarily to leading press organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis is an attempt to explain the behavior of 'leading' press organizations (prestige national newspapers, wire services, television networks, and the 'big three' news magazines) that set professional press standards and influence the daily news agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-audience outlets with ideological missions or local tastes may deviate; conclusions about indexing should primarily be drawn from elite media that function as exemplars for the wider press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor voices: prominent officials and institutional power blocs
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are more likely to index legitimate voices in the news according to the range of views expressed by prominent officials and members of institutional power blocs likely to influence the outcome of a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'official' range is not anchored by fringe government voices but by those institutional actors (senators, cabinet officials, congressional majorities, courts) who are consequential for policy. Evaluations of coverage should check whether news selection maps onto these institutional voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of non-official voices conditioned on parallel official expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Other (i.e., non-official) voices are included in news stories and editorials when those voices express opinions already emerging in official circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess whether non-official voices are genuinely influencing debate (vs. being incidental), check whether their positions mirror or originate within the official debate. If they do not, their presence may be marginal, framed negatively, or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-official voice admissions often occur with negative framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances surrounding such inclusions usually involve civil disobedience, protests, or lawless acts that establish negative interpretative contexts for those voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When social movement or grassroots voices appear only in the context of protest or illegality, their admission into news narratives may be conditioned by negative interpretive frames. Evaluators should note framing distinctions (legitimate vs. criminal context) when measuring 'voice' inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to routine coverage rather than ritual/special coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The indexing hypothesis is intended to apply more to news accounts of everyday events, crises, and policies than to 'special coverage' of things like elections that may have a normative-ritual order of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should separate ordinary policy/crisis reporting from episodic ritualized coverage (e.g., elections) where media practices (like independently reporting polls) differ and may introduce non-official voices irrespective of institutional debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue-area variation in the width of the journalistic gate
rubrics_metrics.description: The range of social voices in the news is likely to vary widely from one issue area to another, perhaps narrowing in areas like foreign affairs and monetary policy and widening in coverage of civil liberties and 'pocketbook' economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations must account for subject-matter differences: expect narrower indexing on national-security/foreign-policy beats and broader inclusion on domestic/personal-impact beats. Use issue-area stratification when measuring voice diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing as a professional rule-of-thumb and justificatory norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing constitutes a quick and ready guide for editors and reporters to use in deciding how to cover a story; it is a rule of thumb that can be defended against questions from uneasy corporate managers and concerned citizens alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing has behavioral, organizational, and attitudinal components: it operates in the newsroom as tacit knowledge, is reinforced by organizational structures (beat systems, reward structures), and is used rhetorically to justify coverage choices. Analytic attention should address all three levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative ideal: balance between government deliberation and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The resulting balance would give governments room to deliberate and maneuver while still holding officials accountable to public opinion in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ideal as an evaluative yardstick: good performance = government afforded space for deliberation + press readiness to publicize popular opposition when institutions exclude or act improperly. Deviations (e.g., consistent marginalization of public opinion) indicate democratic shortfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-analysis measurement dimensions: frequency, direction, and source of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the frequency, direction, and source of all opinions voiced in news and editorials (analyze news accounts and editorial content separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bennett operationalized the hypothesis by coding all Nicaragua-related NYT items over a multi-year period for whether an opinion is voiced, who voiced it, and whether it was supportive, opposed, or ambivalent toward policy. Adopt similar tripartite measurement to test indexing empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories for 'voices' (operational schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voices coded as: editorial and op-ed, administration source, congressional source, judicial source, popular (nongovernmental) source including interest groups and polls, and foreign opinion from U.S. allies. Sandinista and contra opinions were assigned 'no valence' for domestic U.S. policy evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying this scheme, be explicit about treatment of foreign or partisan actors (e.g., actors directly involved in a conflict) and whether their views count toward domestic opinion measures. Note that some index systems may omit polls—search full text databases to retrieve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence coding and equal-weighting rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Valence assigned as + if the voice supported administration policy, - if it opposed the policy, and ± if ambivalent or divided. For the analysis, all coded voices were weighted the same (e.g., the president given same weight as an undersecretary or a poll).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equal-weighting is a methodological choice that simplifies counting but can obscure influence differences; evaluators should document weighting rules and consider sensitivity tests that weight by prominence, office, or circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational coding conventions and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles describing different policy positions were coded as multiple voices (e.g., an article documenting a battle between President Reagan and Speaker O'Neill was double-coded as 'administration voice' and 'congressional voice'); a Senate roll call was coded as a single voice if summarized as a 'victory' or 'loss'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit rules for multi-voiced articles, treat summarized institutional outcomes as single coded voices, and resolve edge cases (passing mentions vs. substantive opinion) with intercoder reliability checks. Note that abstract/index entries may omit some opinion items (like polls), so supplement index searches with full-text database queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic criterion: detect collapse or expansion of official debate and corresponding media response
rubrics_metrics.description: When institutional opposition collapses or official debate narrows, a watchdog press ought to restore democratic balance by amplifying non-official voices; the indexing hypothesis predicts media volume and voice distribution will track the collapse/expansion of official debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests should compare media voice distributions before and after identifiable political shifts (e.g., congressional realignment, policy authorization) to see whether non-official voices increase in prominence when institutions cease to provide contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers and pathways for normative change in news practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible triggers for change include a large market decline for news, loss of public confidence in the media, or a societal political shift (e.g., a turn to the Left) that produces more idealistic reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prospects for press reform, consider structural (market), professional (journalism schools, newsroom culture), and individual (reporter initiative) pathways. Analyses of reform potential should document which external pressures are present and how they interact with internal newsroom norms.
